intro: This branch studies transformations: sliding, flipping, turning and resizing shapes. It gives a precise way to say when two shapes are the same or similar, links geometry to matrices (grids of numbers), and includes a few short proofs where the learner picks the reason for a step.

V.13.01.what: A rigid motion moves a shape without stretching or bending it, so every length and angle stays the same.

levels.a: Matches each point of the original shape with its point in the moved copy (the image).
levels.b: Decides whether a rule is an isometry, a move that keeps every distance the same.
levels.c: Uses the fact that lengths, angles and perimeters stay the same after a rigid motion.
levels.d: Applies a move written as a rule, such as T of (x, y) equals (x + 4, y + 4).

V.13.02.what: A translation slides every point the same distance in the same direction, described by a vector (a pair of numbers for across and up).

levels.a: Reads a vector as so many units across and so many up or down.
levels.b: Slides points of a shape by a given vector.
levels.c: Finds the vector from one point and its image, then uses it on another point.
levels.d: Combines two slides into one, or finds the missing second slide.

V.13.03.what: A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line. The mirror line cuts each point-to-image segment in half at a right angle.

levels.a: Uses the fact that a point and its image are equally far from the mirror.
levels.b: Reflects a point over a horizontal or vertical line.
levels.c: Finds the mirror line from a point and its image.
levels.d: Picks the coordinate rule for a reflection, such as over the line y equals negative x.

V.13.04.what: A rotation turns a shape by an angle around a fixed point, called the center.

levels.a: Matches a counterclockwise turn with the same result clockwise.
levels.b: Picks the coordinate rule for quarter and half turns about the origin.
levels.c: Rotates a point around a center other than the origin.
levels.d: Picks the missing reason in an argument that finds the center of a rotation.
levels.e: Finds the single turn that a slide followed by a turn adds up to.
levels.f: Finds the center of the single turn made by two turns about different points.

V.13.05.what: Doing one transformation after another (a composition). The order often changes the result.

levels.a: Applies two moves in the stated order and sees that order matters.
levels.b: Shows that two reflections add up to a slide or a turn.
levels.c: Names the single move that has the same effect as two moves.
levels.d: Undoes a sequence of moves to find where a point started.
levels.e: Works backwards to find the second mirror line from the resulting slide.
levels.f: Finds the overall effect of a long chain of reflections without doing each one.

V.13.06.what: A glide reflection flips a shape over a line and then slides it along that line, like a trail of footprints.

levels.a: Picks the correct description of a glide reflection.
levels.b: Applies a glide reflection to a point.
levels.c: Names the move that takes one footprint in a trail to another.
levels.d: Names which single move maps one shape onto another in a picture.

V.13.07.what: A shape has symmetry if some flip or turn lands it exactly on itself.

levels.a: Counts the mirror lines (lines of symmetry) of a shape.
levels.b: Counts how many times a shape fits onto itself in one full turn (its order of rotational symmetry).
levels.c: Decides whether a shape has point symmetry, fitting onto itself after a half turn.
levels.d: Works out the symmetries of regular polygons from their number of sides.

V.13.08.what: A dilation enlarges or shrinks a shape from a center point by a scale factor.

levels.a: Multiplies the distance from the center by the scale factor.
levels.b: Dilates points about the origin by multiplying their coordinates.
levels.c: Uses negative scale factors, which flip the image to the other side of the center.
levels.d: Finds the image of a line, which stays parallel to the original.
levels.e: Finds the center and scale factor from a segment and its image.
levels.f: Combines two dilations about different centers into one.

V.13.09.what: Two shapes are congruent (identical in size and shape) if a sequence of rigid motions moves one exactly onto the other.

levels.a: Picks the correct definition of congruence.
levels.b: Picks a sequence of moves that maps one triangle onto another.
levels.c: Recognizes which congruence shortcut a proof using moves is justifying, such as side-angle-side.
levels.d: Finds the exact slide that completes a sequence mapping one triangle onto another.

V.13.10.what: Two shapes are similar (same shape, possibly different size) if a dilation plus rigid motions maps one onto the other.

levels.a: Works out lengths after a dilation and a rigid motion.
levels.b: Picks a sequence of moves that maps one triangle onto a similar one.
levels.c: Picks the reason in the angle-angle similarity proof: dilations keep angles the same.
levels.d: Finds the scale factor between two similar triangles on a grid.

V.13.11.what: A matrix (a grid of numbers) can describe a transformation. Multiplying a point by the matrix moves it.

levels.a: Multiplies a matrix by a point to find its image.
levels.b: Picks the matrix that gives a given reflection or rotation.
levels.c: Uses a matrix that enlarges or shrinks points.
levels.d: Combines two moves by multiplying their matrices, in the right order.

V.13.12.what: A tessellation covers a flat surface with repeating tiles, with no gaps or overlaps.

levels.a: Decides whether one kind of regular polygon can tile on its own.
levels.b: Finds the missing shape in a pattern mixing regular polygons.
levels.c: Checks whether the angles meeting at a corner add up to exactly 360 degrees.
levels.d: Explains why an Escher-style tile, made by moving a cut-out piece, keeps its area and still tiles.
